title: Switch Forwarding & Spanning Tree
summary: See how switches learn and forward frames, why redundant links are dangerous without a protocol to manage them, and how Spanning Tree Protocol prevents loops.

slides.sectionTitle: Redundancy is good until it isn't
slides.markdown: Switches learn addresses automatically and forward frames efficiently — but adding a redundant link for reliability, without anything managing it, can bring down an entire LAN in seconds. **Spanning Tree Protocol** exists to let networks have redundant physical links safely.

A switch builds its MAC address table dynamically, with no configuration required:

- **Learning** — record the source MAC of every incoming frame against the port it arrived on.
- **Flooding** — if the destination MAC isn't in the table yet, send the frame out every port except the one it came in on.
- **Forwarding** — once the destination is known, send the frame out only that one port.

The table has finite size and entries expire (aged out) if unused, so a switch that hasn't heard from a device in a while will flood again the next time — this is normal, not a fault.

Across multiple switches, the same learn/flood/forward logic applies at every hop:

![A frame flooded across three switches, then learned so subsequent frames are forwarded directly](assets/frame-flood-learn.svg)

Only the *first* frame to an unknown destination pays the flooding cost — every switch along the path learns from the reply, and the connection settles into direct forwarding.

assets.alt: A frame flooded across three switches, then learned so subsequent frames are forwarded directly

slides.sectionTitle: Redundant links, broadcast storms, and loops
slides.markdown:
Adding a second cable between two switches for redundancy sounds harmless — until a broadcast frame is sent. With two paths between the same switches, the broadcast loops endlessly: switch A floods it to B, B floods it back toward A (and everywhere else), and neither ever ages the frame out.

Each loop iteration also **duplicates** the frame, so traffic grows exponentially within seconds — a **broadcast storm** that saturates every link and can take the whole LAN offline, often the fastest-growing outage you'll ever see.

**Spanning Tree Protocol (STP)** lets a network keep redundant physical links while guaranteeing no active loop exists:

![A root bridge elected among three switches, with one redundant port blocked to prevent a loop](assets/stp-root-blocking.svg)

Switches elect a single **root bridge** (lowest bridge ID wins), then every other switch computes its shortest path to root and **blocks** any port that would create a second path — the cable stays connected, just logically inactive.

assets.alt: A root bridge elected among three switches, with one redundant port blocked to prevent a loop

slides.markdown:
Classic STP takes up to **30-50 seconds** to converge after a topology change (a link fails, a switch reboots) — it moves through Blocking → Listening → Learning → Forwarding states, each with its own timer, deliberately slow to avoid acting on stale information.

In production, this shows up as a real, visible outage window: a failed redundant link doesn't fail over instantly — traffic can be dropped for tens of seconds while STP recalculates, which is a genuine operational pain point on networks that haven't moved to faster variants.

**RSTP (802.1w)** reworks the state machine to converge in roughly **1-2 seconds** instead of tens — via proposal/agreement handshakes between switches rather than relying purely on timers.

Modern data-center fabrics increasingly skip STP-style blocking altogether for **TRILL** or leaf-spine designs that route around loops at a different layer, since blocking half your redundant capacity is wasteful once you've paid for it.

| | Switch (layer 2) | Router (layer 3) |
|---|---|---|
| Table key | Flat MAC address | Hierarchical IP prefix |
| Built how | Learned automatically from traffic | Configured statically or via routing protocols |
| Scope | One broadcast domain/LAN | Across separate networks |
| Loop risk | Yes — needs STP on redundant links | No — routing protocols detect and avoid loops natively |

**How to decide which one is relevant:** if the question is about forwarding *within* one LAN, think switch/MAC table; if it's about getting between *different* networks, think router/routing table.

slides.subTitle: The redundant link that took down the LAN
slides.markdown:
A classic production incident: someone plugs in an extra cable between two switches "just for redundancy," on a network where STP is disabled or misconfigured. Within seconds, a broadcast storm saturates every link and the entire LAN goes unreachable — often traced back to exactly that one well-intentioned cable.

The fix isn't "never add redundant links" — it's **always verify STP (or an equivalent loop-prevention mechanism) is active** before adding one. Redundancy without loop protection isn't extra safety; it's a live landmine.
